source_note: Aggregated from different Internet sources. Summaries are written in our own words; follow the links for the full stories.

trends.title: Connected cockpits: telematics, local modules and new displays
trends.summary: Berg Insight's latest ranking puts LG Electronics at the top of the telematics control unit market, and LG now says its vehicle electronics unit has become a steady earner as earlier orders reach production. Visteon builds cellular modules in Chennai to supply Indian carmakers locally, and suppliers are exploring the windshield as the next large cockpit display.

items.title: LG's vehicle electronics business steadies while LG Magna struggles with profitability
items.summary: LG Electronics says its automotive electronics business has become a stable earner as orders won earlier turn into revenue. Its electric powertrain joint venture, LG Magna, is still finding profits hard to reach, Chosunbiz reports.
items.script:
Korean business outlet Chosunbiz reports a split picture inside LG's automotive activities. LG Electronics said its automotive electronics business has become a stable source of income, as existing orders are steadily turning into revenue. At the same time, LG Magna, the group's electric powertrain venture, is struggling with profitability. The contrast is useful for anyone following the industry, because it shows that two parts of the same supplier, both working on vehicle electronics, can face very different economics.

Start with how automotive supply contracts work. A supplier usually wins a programme years before the car reaches showrooms. Engineers then spend a long time on development, validation and approval, often called P P A P, before start of production. Revenue only arrives once vehicles are built and sold, and it continues for the life of the model. The total expected value of these awarded contracts is called the order backlog. When a supplier says orders are turning into revenue, it means programmes won in earlier years have finally reached production.

LG's vehicle electronics unit is known for infotainment systems and telematics control units. A telematics control unit contains a cellular modem, a positioning receiver and a secure processor. It handles emergency calls, remote services and over the air updates. Infotainment units run the screens, audio and smartphone integration. These products reuse a lot of consumer electronics know how, from display drivers to wireless design, and their software platforms can be shared across many car brands and models, which spreads development cost.

The electric powertrain business is different. It makes traction motors, inverters and on board chargers. An inverter uses power transistors, made from silicon or silicon carbide, to turn battery direct current into three phase alternating current for the motor. These parts need heavy investment in production lines, are exposed to the ups and downs of electric vehicle demand, and face intense price pressure, especially from Chinese competitors. When electric vehicle volumes grow more slowly than planned, factories run below capacity and margins suffer.

There is a lesson here about business models. Electronics with high software content and broad reuse can earn steady returns. Hardware that is capital intensive and tied to one fast moving market carries more risk, even when the underlying technology is excellent.

For students, it is worth studying how inverters and telematics units are built, and how supplier sourcing cycles work. The full report from Chosunbiz is linked on this page.

items.title: Visteon opens automotive cellular module production line in Chennai
items.summary: Visteon has started building automotive cellular modules at its Chennai factory, so carmakers in India can source a key telematics part locally. The company says the move fits its plan to supply both the connectivity and the cockpit electronics from one vertically integrated operation.
items.script:
Visteon, the cockpit electronics supplier, has launched a new production line for automotive cellular modules at its factory in Chennai, in the Indian state of Tamil Nadu. The expansion was announced on November twenty four. According to the company, local production gives carmakers access to critical vehicle electronics closer to their markets, and it supports the growth of automotive telematics in India. Visteon also says the step strengthens its vertically integrated approach, in which it supplies connectivity hardware and cockpit electronics together rather than as separate parts from separate vendors.

So what is an automotive cellular module, and why does it matter where it is made? The cellular module is the small shielded board that gives a car its link to the mobile network. It contains a modem chip, radio front end circuits, power management and memory, and it runs the protocol stack for four G L T E or five G. Engineers often call it the network access device, or N A D. On its own it does not do much. It is mounted inside a telematics control unit, or T C U, which adds satellite positioning, a backup battery, a connection to the vehicle network over C A N or automotive Ethernet, and security hardware for keys and certificates.

Building these modules is demanding. The parts must meet A E C Q one hundred qualification for automotive temperature and stress. The finished module must pass vibration, thermal cycling and humidity tests, and its radio performance has to be checked on every unit, usually with automated test stations that measure transmit power and receiver sensitivity. The module also has to be certified by mobile network operators and regulators before it can go on sale. Quality systems follow I A T F sixteen nine forty nine, the automotive standard for production.

The module is also the gateway for some of the car's most sensitive functions. Emergency calling, remote diagnostics and over the air software updates all pass through it. That puts the T C U inside the scope of U N regulation one fifty five on cybersecurity and one fifty six on software updates, which carmakers must satisfy for type approval in many markets.

Pairing the modem with the cockpit domain controller in one supplier's hands can simplify integration, because the infotainment software and the connectivity stack are tested together.

For students, this is a good example of how radio engineering, production testing and security meet in one small part. The full report from PR Newswire is linked on this page.

items.title: Berg Insight ranks leading automotive connectivity SoC, NAD and TCU suppliers
items.summary: Analyst firm Berg Insight has ranked the suppliers of connectivity chips, network access devices and telematics control units, putting LG Electronics first among TCU makers with a 27 percent share.
items.script:
The analyst firm Berg Insight has published a ranking of the companies that supply connectivity hardware for cars. The ranking covers three layers of the same product chain: the connectivity chips, the network access devices built around them, and the telematics control units that carmakers fit into their vehicles. According to Berg Insight, LG Electronics is the leading supplier of telematics control units, with a market share of twenty seven percent. The figure was given by Martin Cederqvist, a senior analyst at the firm. TyN Magazine carried the announcement.

It helps to see how a connected car talks to the outside world. The box that does the job is the telematics control unit, or T C U. Inside it sits the network access device, or N A D. This is the cellular modem module, a small shielded board that handles the radio link to the mobile network. And at the heart of the N A D is the connectivity S o C, the chip that runs the modem protocol stack for four G L T E or five G.

Each layer adds work. The chip vendor delivers the baseband processor and the radio front end. The module maker qualifies that chip for automotive use, which means temperature cycling, vibration testing and A E C Q one hundred qualified components. The T C U supplier then adds the parts that make it a car product: a satellite positioning receiver, a backup battery, an interface to the vehicle network over C A N or automotive Ethernet, and a hardware security module for keys and certificates.

The T C U carries some of the most important functions in a modern car. In Europe it delivers e Call, the automatic emergency call that has been required on new car types since twenty eighteen. It is also the path for over the air software updates, remote diagnostics and connected services. That makes it a prime target for attackers, so its design falls under U N regulation one fifty five on cybersecurity and one fifty six on software updates.

The technology is also moving. Mobile operators are switching off two G and three G networks, which pushes carmakers towards four G and five G modules and towards next generation e Call over L T E.

For students, the T C U is a good case study in how one E C U ties together radio engineering, security and embedded software. The full report from TyN Magazine is linked on this page.

items.title: LG Electronics wins PACE Pilot award for UltraView Windshield Display
items.summary: LG Electronics received a 2026 Automotive News PACE Pilot award for its UltraView Windshield Display, a windshield-based display that is still at an early stage and not yet in production.
items.script:
LG Electronics has won a twenty twenty six Automotive News PACE Pilot award for a product called the UltraView Windshield Display. The PACE awards recognise supplier innovation in the car industry, and the Pilot category is meant for technology that is promising but not yet in series production. That matches how LG's display was described: an early stage technology that has not yet reached the market. The award places the display among the new ideas that carmakers are weighing for future cabins. TradingView carried the news.

So what does it take to turn a windshield into a display? The most common approach today is the head up display, or H U D. A small unit buried in the dashboard contains a picture generation unit. This can be a backlit T F T L C D panel, a D L P micromirror chip, or a laser scanner. The image is folded by one or two mirrors and thrown onto the windshield, which acts as a partial mirror and reflects it towards the driver's eyes. The driver sees a virtual image that seems to float some distance ahead of the car, so the eyes do not need to refocus between the road and the display.

There are hard engineering problems hidden in that simple picture. A windshield has two glass surfaces, and each one reflects, so a plain windshield produces a double image. Carmakers fix this with a wedge shaped plastic interlayer inside the laminated glass, which brings the two reflections back together. Brightness is another challenge. The image has to stay readable against bright sky and snow, so the picture source must be extremely bright, and the optics must survive sunlight being focused back into them.

Augmented reality H U Ds push this further. They place the virtual image further down the road, so that navigation arrows and lane markings can be laid over the real scene. That needs larger optics, a wider field of view and a tight link to the A D A S sensors and to the vehicle's position.

The next step, which awards like this one point towards, is to use much more of the glass. Ideas include projecting onto large areas of the windshield, transparent display layers and special reflective films. Each brings new questions about driver distraction, optical quality, and how the glass is repaired or replaced after damage.

If you want to go deeper, study H U D optics, virtual image distance, and how the display controller connects to the cockpit domain computer. The full report from TradingView is linked on this page.

trends.title: Driver assistance: centralised radar and low-cost self-driving
trends.summary: Radar chips are being redesigned for centralised architectures, where a central computer processes data from lean sensor front ends, as in Infineon's new four-transmit, four-receive RASIC. At the same time, China is pushing advanced driver assistance into affordable cars, shown by a roughly 18,000-dollar Volkswagen sedan developed in China for Chinese buyers.

items.title: Infineon introduces 4Tx/4Rx RASIC radar MMIC for centralised automotive radar
items.summary: Infineon's new RASIC CTRX8144FS is a 76 to 81 GHz radar chip with four transmit and four receive channels, aimed at radar systems whose processing sits in a central computer. On-chip diagnostics keep watch on RF performance and die temperature to support functional safety.
items.script:
Infineon has added a new RASIC automotive radar chip. The part is called the C T R X eight one four four F S. It is a radar M M I C, which stands for monolithic microwave integrated circuit, and it works in the seventy six to eighty one gigahertz band. It packs four transmit channels and four receive channels onto one chip. Infineon positions it for centralised radar architectures. Reports say its low thermal resistance lets it run across the full automotive temperature range, and built in diagnostics continuously monitor radio frequency performance and internal temperatures.

So what does a chip like this actually do? A radar M M I C is the analogue heart of a radar sensor. It generates a rising frequency ramp, called a chirp, and sends it out through the transmit antennas. Echoes from cars, pedestrians and guard rails return to the receive antennas. The chip mixes each echo with the signal it is sending at that moment. The small difference in frequency, called the beat frequency, is proportional to distance. Phase shifts between chirps reveal speed through the Doppler effect. This scheme is called F M C W, or frequency modulated continuous wave radar.

Four transmitters and four receivers can form sixteen virtual channels, as long as the transmit signals are coded so the receiver can tell them apart. This is known as M I M O radar, short for multiple input, multiple output. More virtual channels give a larger virtual antenna and finer angular resolution. That helps separate a motorbike riding beside a truck.

The word centralised matters too. In a classic design, every radar module carries its own processor and sends out a finished list of objects. In a centralised design, the sensor behind the bumper becomes a leaner front end. It digitises the echoes and streams lower level data over a fast link to a central A D A S computer. That computer can fuse several radars with cameras and improve through software updates.

Safety is a big part of the story. Radar feeds functions such as automatic emergency braking and adaptive cruise control, so the hardware is developed under I S O twenty six two six two. Continuous self checks let the system notice a degraded sensor and react safely.

For students, this is a good moment to study F M C W signal processing, range and Doppler F F T s, and M I M O array design. The full report from TimesTech is linked on this page.

items.title: VW's $18,000 self-driving sedan shows how China leads on car technology
items.summary: Bloomberg looks at a low-cost Volkswagen sedan with self-driving features whose technology, including its plug-in hybrid drivetrain, was developed in China for Chinese buyers. Volkswagen is reported to be weighing wider use of the same technology.
items.script:
Bloomberg has published an analysis built around a new Volkswagen sedan for China. The car is priced at around eighteen thousand dollars, yet it is marketed with self driving features. According to the report, the car's technology, including its plug in hybrid drivetrain, was developed in China, for China. Volkswagen is said to be considering deploying that technology beyond the car itself. Bloomberg presents the model as evidence of how far China now leads on car technology, especially in packing advanced features into affordable vehicles.

Why is this technically interesting? A few years ago, driver assistance at this level was reserved for premium cars. The cost has fallen because of how the electronics are now organised. Instead of many small control units, each with its own sensor, a modern system uses one A D A S domain controller. This is a powerful computer built around an automotive system on chip with dedicated neural network accelerators. Cameras, radar and sometimes lidar all feed into it. One software stack handles lane keeping, adaptive cruise, automated parking and navigation on highways and city roads.

It helps to know the vocabulary. The S A E J thirty sixteen standard defines driving automation from level zero to level five. Most so called self driving features sold to consumers today are level two. The car steers, brakes and accelerates, but the driver must supervise at all times. Calling a feature self driving does not change that legal responsibility.

The plug in hybrid side is just as relevant. A plug in hybrid pairs a petrol engine with a battery large enough for everyday electric driving, plus an on board charger. Chinese designs often use dedicated hybrid transmissions, where one or two electric motors do most of the work and the engine acts mainly as a generator. Power electronics, the inverter and the battery management system, carry much of the engineering.

The bigger theme is development speed. Volkswagen has in recent years partnered with Chinese technology companies and set up local engineering teams. The aim is to shorten development cycles from many years to a much shorter time, a pace often described as China speed. Software defined architectures, local chip suppliers and aggressive cost targets all play a part.

For engineers, this is a reminder that cost engineering of sensors, compute and power electronics is now as important as raw performance. Studying centralised E and E architectures is a good next step. The full report from Bloomberg is linked on this page.

trends.title: Software-defined vehicles are pulling engineering work into India
trends.summary: Global suppliers keep adding Indian engineering capacity for software-defined mobility, cybersecurity and virtual validation, mostly in Bengaluru and Pune. Indian firms are building AI toolchains such as L&T Technology Services' SDVault.ai, Synopsys warns that carmakers must keep control of their software, and the government's PLI Auto scheme continues to back local production of advanced automotive technology.

items.title: Synopsys: carmakers risk losing their products' soul without software control
items.summary: Speaking to Autocar Professional, Synopsys executive Subramanian warns that carmakers who give up control of vehicle software risk losing what makes their products distinct. He adds that OEMs are themselves pushing technology firms to collaborate and deliver integrated engineering.
items.script:
Autocar Professional has carried comments from Synopsys, the chip design and simulation software company, on who should control software in tomorrow's cars. The headline message is blunt. Carmakers risk losing their products' soul if they do not keep control of their software. According to the report, Subramanian of Synopsys also said that automotive manufacturers themselves are encouraging technology companies to collaborate and deliver integrated engineering, rather than isolated tools and parts.

Why would software be the soul of a car? In a software defined vehicle, many things that drivers feel are decided in code. Steering feel, throttle response, regenerative braking, the look of the screens and the behaviour of driver assistance are all tuned by software. If a carmaker buys a complete black box from a supplier, every car using that box can start to feel the same. Keeping the software in house, or at least owning its architecture and key functions, protects brand identity and lets the company keep improving the car through over the air updates.

Controlling software is hard, though. A modern car runs code from many sources on a mix of microcontrollers and high performance computers. Standards help keep this manageable. Classic and Adaptive AUTOSAR define how software components talk to each other and to the hardware. A S P I C E describes mature development processes. I S O twenty six two six two covers functional safety, and I S O twenty one four three four covers cybersecurity.

This is where companies like Synopsys come in. Their tools let engineers build a virtual E C U, a software model of the real control unit, including its processor. Real production code can run on this model on an ordinary computer or in the cloud, long before physical hardware exists. Testing early in this way is called shift left. Thousands of test scenarios can run automatically every night as part of continuous integration. Virtual models of chips also let carmakers and chip makers agree on requirements earlier, which matters as more carmakers design or specify their own silicon.

The call for integrated engineering reflects a real pain point. Hardware, software and system teams often work with separate tools and timelines, and problems often show up late, during integration on real vehicles, when fixes are most expensive.

For students, learning AUTOSAR, virtual prototyping and continuous integration for embedded code is valuable. The full report from Autocar Professional is linked on this page.

items.title: Government outlines PLI scheme for automobiles and auto components
items.summary: A Government of India press release sets out the production-linked incentive scheme for vehicles and auto components. The scheme aims to strengthen domestic manufacturing, promote advanced automotive technologies and position India as a global hub for the sector.
items.script:
The Press Information Bureau, the Government of India's official news service, has issued a release on the production linked incentive scheme for the automobile and auto component industry, usually called P L I Auto. According to the release, the scheme aims to enhance domestic manufacturing capabilities, promote advanced automotive technologies and position India as a global hub for the sector. The release adds to recent news on this page, such as Toyota's hybrid expansion in India under the same programme.

How does a production linked incentive work? Instead of paying money up front, the government pays companies a percentage of their additional sales of qualifying products, once those products are actually made in India. To qualify, companies must commit to investment, meet sales thresholds and show that a large share of the value is added locally. The idea is to reward real production and sales rather than promises, so public money follows actual output.

The auto version of the scheme focuses on what it calls advanced automotive technology products. In practice, this means the parts that are hardest to source locally today. Electric drive components are one group, including traction motors, inverters, battery packs and battery management systems. Electronics for safety and driver assistance are another, including sensors, radar, cameras and electronic control units. Many of these depend on semiconductors, printed circuit boards and specialised assembly lines that India has historically imported.

For an engineer, localisation is not only about building a factory. A locally made E C U still needs automotive grade chips qualified to A E C Q one hundred, boards made to tight reliability rules, and a quality system certified to I A T F sixteen nine four nine. Each new supplier must pass the carmaker's production part approval process before parts reach a vehicle. Building this ecosystem takes years, and incentives help bridge the gap while volumes grow.

The policy also links to India's wider electronics and semiconductor programmes. As cars carry more electronics, the value of the electronic content rises sharply, and a country that only assembles mechanical parts captures less of that value. That is why incentives increasingly target electronics, software and electrified powertrains rather than traditional components.

For students, it is worth understanding how automotive quality systems and component qualification work, since these skills are central to any localisation effort. The full report from the Press Information Bureau is linked on this page.

items.title: Manoj Kumar Panda to lead VECV's embedded technology, connectivity and SDV work
items.summary: VE Commercial Vehicles has put Manoj Kumar Panda in charge of its embedded technology, connectivity and software-defined vehicle programmes. He previously worked at CEER, FEV and Tata Motors and has more than 26 years in automotive electronics and vehicle architecture.
items.script:
VE Commercial Vehicles, the Indian truck and bus maker known as V E C V, has appointed Manoj Kumar Panda to lead its embedded technology, connectivity and software defined vehicle initiatives. Autocar Professional reported the move. Panda has previously worked at CEER, at the engineering firm F E V and at Tata Motors, and he brings more than twenty six years of experience in automotive electronics and vehicle architecture. The source article could not be opened for this overview, so the facts are taken from its published summary. The rest explains why such a role matters.

Commercial vehicles are going through the same electronic shift as passenger cars, but with different priorities. A truck operator cares about uptime, fuel cost and fleet management. That makes connectivity especially valuable. A telematics unit on a truck can report location, fuel use, driver behaviour and fault codes to a fleet portal in real time. Engineers can read diagnostic trouble codes remotely, plan maintenance before a breakdown and, increasingly, push software updates over the air.

Embedded technology is the base of all this. Every function, from engine and transmission control to brakes and body electronics, runs on E C Us with real time software. In heavy vehicles, these E C Us often talk over C A N using the S A E J nineteen thirty nine protocol, which defines standard messages for engines, transmissions and brakes. Newer designs add automotive Ethernet for cameras and higher bandwidth data.

A software defined vehicle takes this further. Instead of dozens of separate boxes, each with fixed software, the architecture moves towards a few powerful central or zonal computers. Functions become software applications that can be updated, added or improved during the vehicle's life. That requires a clear separation between hardware and software, middleware such as AUTOSAR, and a secure update chain. Regulations such as U N regulation one fifty five on cybersecurity and one fifty six on software updates apply to trucks and buses as well as cars.

For a commercial vehicle maker, the business case is strong. Software features can improve fuel efficiency, safety and service revenue across a fleet that runs for many years. Predictive maintenance, remote fault analysis and features that can be switched on after sale all depend on a well designed electronic architecture underneath.

Leadership roles like this show where the industry is hiring: people who understand both vehicle architecture and software. The full report from Autocar Professional is linked on this page.

items.title: Tech firm claims AI-led virtual twins can deliver 10x engineering gains for OEMs
items.summary: A technology company tells ET Auto that AI-driven virtual twins can make vehicle engineering ten times faster and help established carmakers keep up with Chinese development speed. The 10x figure is the company's own claim, framed against the pressure of SDVs and fast electrification.
items.script:
ET Auto has published an interview with a technology company that says A I led virtual twins can deliver ten times gains in engineering productivity. The company argues that this could help established carmakers match what the industry calls China speed, the much shorter development cycles of Chinese manufacturers. The pitch is set against the pressure created by software defined vehicles and rapid electrification. The source article could not be opened for this overview, so the details come from its published summary. Keep in mind that the ten times figure is the company's own claim.

What is a virtual twin? It is a digital model of a product that behaves like the real one closely enough to be used for engineering decisions. In vehicle development it can describe the mechanical structure, the thermal behaviour of a battery, the dynamics of the chassis, or the electronics and software that control them. Engineers test the model instead of waiting for physical prototypes, which are expensive and arrive late.

For electronics and software, the key methods have names worth knowing. Model in the loop tests control algorithms as simulation models. Software in the loop runs the real compiled code on a computer against a simulated vehicle. Hardware in the loop connects a real E C U to a real time simulator that pretends to be the rest of the car, feeding it sensor signals and reading its outputs. A virtual E C U goes one step further and runs the production software on a simulated processor, so testing can start before the hardware exists.

Where does A I come in? Simulation produces huge amounts of data. Machine learning can build fast surrogate models that approximate slow physics simulations, suggest test cases that are most likely to find faults, and help engineers sort through results. For driver assistance, A I is also used to generate realistic traffic scenarios.

There are limits. A twin is only as good as its validation against real measurements, and safety standards such as I S O twenty six two six two expect clear evidence that simulation tools are trustworthy. Physical testing does not disappear. It becomes more targeted. Prototype vehicles are then used mainly to confirm what the models predicted and to calibrate them for the next round of work.

Virtual validation is one of the fastest growing skills in automotive engineering. The full report from ET Auto is linked on this page.

items.title: L&T Technology Services launches AI platform for software-defined vehicle engineering
items.summary: L&T Technology Services has launched SDVault.ai, an AI-based engineering toolchain meant to help carmakers and Tier-1 suppliers develop, integrate and validate software for software-defined vehicles across the V-cycle.
items.script:
The Indian engineering services company L and T Technology Services has launched a new platform called S D Vault dot A I. According to E T Auto and other trade outlets, it is an A I powered engineering toolchain. It is designed to help carmakers and tier one suppliers develop, integrate and validate software for software defined vehicles. The company presents it as a way to bring engineering intelligence to the whole V cycle. This story reached us as a short alert, so the platform's modules and claims are described in the linked report.

To understand the pitch, start with the V model. It is the classic way automotive software is built. On the left side of the V, engineers move downwards from vehicle requirements to system architecture, then software design, then code. On the right side, they climb back up, testing units, integrating them, and finally validating the complete vehicle against the original requirements. Every test on the right must trace back to a requirement on the left.

That traceability is demanded by the process standards. Automotive S P I C E assesses how mature a supplier's development process is. I S O twenty six two six two covers functional safety, and I S O twenty one four three four covers cybersecurity. Each one produces large volumes of documents, reviews and evidence.

In a software defined vehicle, the problem grows. Functions move from many small E C U s into a few powerful central computers. Software is updated over the air for years after the sale. So the V cycle is no longer run once per car program. It runs again and again.

This is where A I tools are being applied across the industry. Language models can check requirements for ambiguity, suggest test cases, and keep trace links up to date. Virtual E C U s and software in the loop testing let teams validate code on servers long before hardware exists, with hardware in the loop rigs reserved for final checks. This shortens the loop between writing a change and knowing whether it breaks something.

The open question for any such platform is trust. Safety standards require that tools used in development are qualified, and A I outputs must still be reviewed by engineers.

For students, learning the V model, traceability and virtual validation is the best preparation for this kind of work. The full report from E T Auto is linked on this page.

items.title: thyssenkrupp Automotive Technology opens Pune engineering centre, plans 300-plus workforce
items.summary: The new capability centre already has more than 120 engineers on software-defined mobility, cybersecurity and advanced chassis work, and plans to pass 300.
items.script:
thyssenkrupp Automotive Technology has opened a new engineering centre in Pune. The company calls it a global capability centre. It already employs more than one hundred and twenty engineers, and the plan is to grow beyond three hundred. The work there covers three areas: software-defined mobility, cybersecurity, and advanced chassis systems.

Let's unpack why those three areas sit together. thyssenkrupp is best known in automotive for steering systems and dampers, the mechanical heart of the chassis. But a modern steering system is no longer just a column, a rack and a hydraulic pump. Electric power steering uses a motor, a torque sensor and an electronic control unit that decides how much assistance to give at every moment. The next step is steer-by-wire, where there is no mechanical link between the steering wheel and the road wheels at all. The driver's input becomes a stream of data, and actuators at the front axle turn the wheels.

Once steering becomes software and data, two things follow. First, the function can be updated and improved over the life of the vehicle, which is the core idea of the software-defined vehicle. Second, it becomes a target. If an attacker could inject false messages onto the network that carries steering commands, the consequences would be severe. That is why cybersecurity engineers now sit next to chassis engineers. Standards such as I S O twenty one four three four and the U N regulation R one five five require carmakers and suppliers to analyse threats, protect communication with techniques like secure onboard communication, and monitor vehicles in the field.

Chassis functions are also safety critical, so the same software must satisfy functional safety under I S O twenty six two six two. Steer-by-wire typically needs redundant sensors, redundant power supplies and fail-operational designs, meaning the system must keep working safely even after a fault.

Why Pune? India has become one of the largest pools of automotive software and validation talent in the world. Many European and American suppliers now run their embedded software, model-based development, simulation and testing from Indian centres, often working around the clock with teams in Europe.

For engineers and students, the message is clear. Skills that combine embedded software, vehicle networks, functional safety and cybersecurity are in demand, and the jobs are increasingly being created here in India. If you are studying chassis control, it is worth learning how those systems communicate and how they are protected, not just how they are tuned.

You can read the full report on E T Auto using the link on this page.

items.title: Auto manufacturing needs greater R&D investment to tap next growth phase: CII chairman
items.summary: CII argues that electronics, software and AI are converging with mechanical engineering, so Indian suppliers need to spend more on R&D.
items.script:
The chairman of the Confederation of Indian Industry has called for much greater investment in research and development by India's automotive manufacturers. The argument is that the next phase of growth will depend on technology, as electronics, software, artificial intelligence, advanced materials and mechanical engineering converge and change both the products and the way they are made.

Why is this convergence such a big deal? For most of the last century, a car's value was mainly mechanical: the engine, the transmission, the body and the suspension. Indian manufacturing grew strong by building these parts at scale and at low cost. Today, a growing share of a vehicle's cost and value sits in electronics and software. A modern car can carry dozens of electronic control units, several kilometres of wiring, cameras, radar sensors and a central computer running millions of lines of code. In an electric vehicle, the battery, the motor controller and the power electronics can make up a large part of the bill of materials.

This shift changes what it means to be a competitive supplier. Building a part to a drawing is no longer enough. Carmakers increasingly want suppliers who can design the system, write the software, validate it and keep updating it. That requires engineering teams, test labs, simulation tools and long development cycles, all of which need sustained research spending.

The manufacturing side is changing too. Factories use more sensors, data and A I to predict machine failures, check quality with cameras and plan production. So the same digital skills are needed on the shop floor as in the vehicle.

India has an advantage in software talent, and global companies already run large engineering centres here. A point often made by industry observers is that much of that work is done for foreign companies, and that many Indian component makers invest less of their revenue in their own research than their global peers. Building intellectual property, rather than only providing engineering services, is seen as the way to capture more value.

Government programmes such as the production linked incentive scheme for automobiles and auto components, and the semiconductor mission, are meant to support this. But the message from industry bodies is that private investment must rise as well.

For students and young engineers, this is encouraging. It suggests that demand will keep growing for people who understand electronics, embedded software, power electronics and data, and who can connect them with mechanical design.

The full article from E T Manufacturing is linked on this page.

items.title: SDVs, AI and virtual engineering emerge as key drivers of India's automotive engineering shift
items.summary: Industry speakers describe vehicles that are updated over the air and validated virtually, and what that changes in engineering teams.
items.script:
Software-defined vehicles, artificial intelligence and virtual engineering are emerging as the main forces reshaping automotive engineering in India. Industry leaders described how carmakers and technology companies are preparing for vehicles that are updated continuously, validated virtually and adapted over their lifetime.

Let's start with the software-defined vehicle, or S D V. In a traditional car, each function lives in its own electronic control unit with its own fixed software. Adding a feature often means adding another box. In a software-defined vehicle, the electrical and electronic architecture is reorganised around a few powerful central computers and zone controllers. Functions become software applications that can be added or improved through over-the-air updates, long after the car leaves the factory. Middleware such as adaptive AUTOSAR and service-oriented communication like SOME over I P make this possible.

This has a big consequence for testing. If software keeps changing, you cannot rely only on physical prototypes and test drives to validate each release. That is where virtual engineering comes in. Engineers build digital models of the vehicle, its sensors and its environment, and run software against them. You may have heard the terms model in the loop, software in the loop and hardware in the loop. Together they let teams test thousands of scenarios automatically, including dangerous ones that would be impossible to try on a real road. Digital twins extend this idea by keeping a virtual copy of a real vehicle or system that is updated with field data.

Artificial intelligence plays several roles. It powers perception in driver assistance systems, it helps generate and prioritise test cases, it can assist engineers in writing and reviewing code, and it can analyse data coming back from vehicles in the field.

Why does this matter for India in particular? Indian engineering centres already carry out a large share of the world's automotive software development and validation. As the industry moves toward continuous software delivery and virtual testing, the skills in demand shift toward cloud tooling, continuous integration pipelines, simulation, and of course the safety and cybersecurity processes that keep updates trustworthy.

For students, a practical takeaway: learn how the V-model maps onto continuous integration, get comfortable with simulation tools, and understand how over-the-air updates are secured. Those are the building blocks of the software-defined vehicle.

You can read the full feature on E T Auto through the link on this page.

trends.title: Power electronics and electrified powertrains
trends.summary: Better high-voltage DC/DC conversion, hybrids built for several powertrain options, isolated drivers for solid-state relays and higher-power LIN motor drivers for smart actuators. Toyota is also expanding hybrid production in India under the PLI scheme, and Formula E remains a test bed for inverter and motor technology.

items.title: Melexis launches fourth-generation automotive LIN motor drivers
items.summary: Melexis has added the MLX81352 and MLX81354 to its range of LIN motor driver chips. The fourth-generation parts target small smart actuators that need more power than earlier devices could deliver.
items.script:
Melexis, the Belgian chip maker, has introduced two new automotive motor driver chips, the M L X eight one three five two and the M L X eight one three five four. They are the fourth generation of the company's L I N motor drivers. According to Electronics Weekly, the new parts are aimed at mechatronic applications that need more power than earlier generations could handle. The story came through as a short alert, so the detailed figures for the two chips are in the linked report.

To see why such chips matter, think about how many small motors a modern car contains. There are flaps in the climate control system, coolant and oil pumps, cooling fans, active grille shutters, seat adjusters and headlamp levellers. Each one needs a little bit of intelligence, but none of them justifies a full electronic control unit of its own.

The answer is the smart actuator. The electronics are built straight into the motor housing, and a single chip does almost everything. It contains a small microcontroller, a voltage regulator that runs from the twelve volt supply, a driver stage for the motor, and a L I N transceiver for talking to the rest of the car.

L I N stands for Local Interconnect Network. It is standardised as I S O seventeen nine eight seven. It uses a single wire, runs at up to about twenty kilobits per second, and follows a simple commander and responder scheme. A body or zone controller sends a command, and the actuator replies with its status. It is far cheaper than C A N, which makes it ideal for slow, low cost functions.

Many of these actuators now use brushless D C motors. They last longer and run more quietly than brushed motors, but they need electronic commutation. The chip must switch the motor phases in the right order, often without a position sensor, by measuring the back E M F the spinning motor produces. Better parts use field oriented control for smooth, quiet torque.

Higher power brings new problems. More current means more heat in a small, sealed housing, and stronger protection against short circuits, over voltage and load dumps. The chips must also pass A E C Q one hundred qualification, and many functions now need a safety analysis under I S O twenty six two six two.

For students, a L I N smart actuator is a compact lesson in embedded control, motor drives and vehicle networking in one package. The full report from Electronics Weekly is linked on this page.

items.title: Toyota India bets big on hybrids, to add 2 lakh units of capacity
items.summary: Toyota's Indian arm plans to add capacity for about two lakh more vehicles a year with a strong focus on hybrids. The project is tied to the Advanced Automotive Technology category of India's production-linked incentive scheme.
items.script:
Toyota's Indian business is placing a large bet on hybrid cars. According to Team B H P, the company plans to add production capacity of two lakh units, which is two hundred thousand vehicles. The report links the project to the Advanced Automotive Technology category of the Indian government's production linked incentive scheme for automobiles and auto components. This story reached us as a short alert, so the investment figures and timelines are in the linked article.

Let us look at what makes a strong hybrid work, because that is where most of the electronics sit. Toyota's system is a power split hybrid. A planetary gear set connects three things: the petrol engine, a smaller motor generator, and a larger traction motor that drives the wheels. By controlling the speed of the small motor generator, the system acts like a continuously variable transmission. The engine can run at its most efficient speed, while the electric side fills the gaps.

The heart of the electronics is the power control unit. It contains a boost converter that raises the battery voltage to several hundred volts, and two inverters, one for each motor. The inverters use power transistors, switching thousands of times a second, to turn direct current into three phase alternating current. When the car slows down, the process runs in reverse, and braking energy flows back into the battery.

The battery itself is small compared with a full electric car, usually around one kilowatt hour. It is built for high power and many shallow cycles rather than long range. A battery management system watches every cell's voltage and temperature, balances the cells, and keeps the state of charge inside a narrow window so the pack lasts for the life of the car.

Above all of this sits the hybrid control software. It decides, many times a second, how to split the driver's torque request between engine and motors, and when to start or stop the engine smoothly. It also has to manage heat in the motors and inverters, because the power transistors lose efficiency and age faster when they run hot.

The incentive scheme matters too. It rewards products classed as advanced automotive technology, and it expects a high share of value to be added in India. That pushes motors, inverters and battery packs towards local manufacture, which creates work for Indian power electronics engineers.

For students, the power split hybrid is a classic case study in mechanical and electrical co design. The full report from Team B H P is linked on this page.

items.title: Flex Wins 2026 Automotive News PACE Award for Fully Symmetric HV DC/DC Architecture
items.summary: The award-winning DC/DC design aims to simplify the vehicle's electrical architecture and reduce dependence on the auxiliary low-voltage network.
items.script:
Flex has won a 2026 Automotive News PACE Award for its high voltage D C to D C converter for electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles. The PACE Awards are judged by an independent panel and recognise supplier innovations with real technical and business impact. Flex says this is its third PACE Award in two years. An earlier one recognised a backup D C to D C converter that keeps essential drive-by-wire systems powered.

First, what does a D C to D C converter do in an electric car? The traction battery runs at around four hundred or eight hundred volts. But lights, infotainment, control units, pumps and fans still run from a low voltage network, usually twelve volts. The D C to D C converter steps the high voltage down to supply that network, and it replaces the alternator you would find in a petrol car.

Flex describes its design as fully symmetric, based on a dual active bridge topology. Here is the idea. You have two full bridges of power transistors, one on each side of a high-frequency transformer. Each bridge switches at high frequency, and the power flow is controlled by the phase shift between them. Because the two sides are built the same way, power can flow in either direction. The transformer also provides galvanic isolation, which is essential for safety, so the high voltage side is electrically separated from the low voltage side the occupants can touch.

Flex says the converter accepts a wide input voltage range, works with both four hundred and eight hundred volt batteries, supports bidirectional energy flow and responds quickly to changing loads. It can also be integrated with onboard chargers, inverters and software-based power management.

Why does bidirectional flow matter? It means the low voltage side can be supported directly from the high voltage battery, and in some cases energy can flow back the other way. Flex claims this reduces reliance on the auxiliary twelve volt battery, simplifies the electrical architecture, saves weight and cost and improves reliability. As vehicles adopt by-wire steering and braking, keeping the low voltage supply stable becomes a safety issue, not just a convenience.

For students of power electronics, the dual active bridge is a great example of how topology choice drives system benefits. Look up soft switching, phase-shift control and isolation requirements to go deeper.

The full press release from Flex is linked on this page.

items.title: Growth of the Automotive Power Electronics Market Driven by EVs
items.summary: A market report linking growth in automotive power electronics to EV adoption. It is promotional, so read the figures with caution.
items.script:
A new market report says the automotive power electronics sector is growing quickly as it adapts to the rapid rise of electric vehicles and advanced vehicle systems. Reports like this are published by market research firms to promote their full studies, so their forecasts should be read with some caution. But the underlying trend is real, and worth understanding.

So what counts as power electronics in a vehicle? It is the hardware that converts and controls electrical energy. In an electric car, the main pieces are the traction inverter, which turns the battery's direct current into alternating current to drive the motor; the onboard charger, which converts alternating current from the grid into direct current for the battery; and the D C to D C converter, which steps the high voltage down to supply the twelve volt network. Even in petrol cars, power electronics drive electric power steering, fuel pumps, cooling fans and L E D lighting.

At the heart of all of these are power semiconductor switches. For decades, the workhorses were silicon M O S F E Ts and I G B Ts. Now, wide bandgap materials are taking over in high-voltage applications. Silicon carbide transistors can block higher voltages, switch faster and run hotter with lower losses. That is why many eight hundred volt electric cars use silicon carbide in their inverters. Gallium nitride is gaining ground in lower-power converters and onboard chargers, where very fast switching allows smaller magnetic components.

Why do these choices matter? Every percent of efficiency in the inverter becomes extra driving range, or a smaller battery for the same range. Lower losses also mean less heat, so cooling systems can be smaller and lighter. Faster switching shrinks inductors and capacitors, reducing the size and cost of the whole unit.

The challenges are also real. Fast switching creates electromagnetic interference that must be filtered. High temperatures stress solder joints and packages, so reliability engineering is a big part of the job. And control software, from pulse width modulation to protection logic, has to be fast and functionally safe.

For students, power electronics is one of the most valuable skill sets in the E V era. Start with buck and boost converters, then study inverters, gate drivers and thermal design.

The market report is linked on this page; treat its numbers as indicative.

items.title: Toshiba launches photovoltaic-output photocoupler for automotive relays
items.summary: Toshiba has introduced the TLX9909, an optically isolated device that generates its own gate voltage to switch MOSFET-based solid-state relays in vehicle equipment.
items.script:
Toshiba has launched a new part for automotive equipment called the T L X ninety nine oh nine. It is a photovoltaic-output photocoupler. Its job is to drive solid-state relays, often shortened to S S Rs, which replace mechanical relays in a vehicle. The announcement was reported by P V Magazine. The short alert we received did not list electrical ratings or a shipping date, so we will not guess at those. Instead, let's look at how this kind of device works and why carmakers want it.

Start with the problem. A relay lets a small control signal switch a much larger load, while keeping the two circuits apart. A classic electromechanical relay uses a coil and moving contacts. It is cheap and robust, but contacts wear, they bounce, they can arc, and they click. A solid-state relay does the same job with semiconductors, usually two power MOSFETs connected back to back so they can block current in both directions.

The tricky part is driving those MOSFETs. Their gates must be lifted several volts above their sources, and in a high-voltage system the sources may float hundreds of volts away from the low-voltage control electronics. That is where a photovoltaic-output photocoupler comes in. On the input side there is an infrared L E D. On the output side there is a stack of tiny photodiodes connected in series, acting like a miniature solar cell. When the L E D lights up, the photodiode stack generates a small voltage on its own, with no isolated power supply needed. That voltage charges the MOSFET gates and turns the relay on. When the L E D switches off, an internal discharge circuit pulls the gates down and the relay opens.

The light path is the isolation barrier. There is no electrical connection between the microcontroller side and the switched side, which is what designers call galvanic isolation. Package design matters a lot here, because creepage and clearance distances decide how much voltage the barrier can safely withstand over the life of the car.

In electric vehicles, isolated switches like these are commonly used around the battery, for example in insulation-resistance monitoring and in battery management circuits. For automotive use, optoelectronic parts are normally qualified to A E C Q one oh two stress tests.

To go further, study MOSFET gate charge, turn-on time and isolation coordination. The full report from P V Magazine is linked on this page.

items.title: Mahindra Racing strengthens GEN4 technical programme with Valeo as Official Performance and Engineering Partner
items.summary: Valeo brings its electrification know-how to Mahindra's Formula E GEN4 programme.
items.script:
Mahindra Racing has named Valeo as its official performance and engineering partner for the Formula E GEN4 era. The partnership builds on an existing relationship: Valeo already supplies electric axles for Mahindra's road vehicles. For racing, the work focuses on two areas: software for motor control, and hardware testing of the powertrain components. Mahindra's GEN4 car is called the M13 Electro. Valeo's work will be led mainly from its research labs and advanced technology centre in Erlangen, Germany.

Let's look at what motor control software actually does. A racing electric motor is typically a permanent magnet synchronous machine, driven by an inverter that converts the battery's direct current into three-phase alternating current. The control algorithm, usually field-oriented control, measures the rotor position and the phase currents thousands of times per second. It then decides exactly how to switch the inverter's transistors so the magnetic field in the stator stays at the right angle to the rotor. Get it right and you get maximum torque for every amp. Get it slightly wrong and you waste energy as heat.

In Formula E, energy is strictly limited, so efficiency decides races. Valeo is developing custom control algorithms to manage the motor precisely, optimise energy use and reduce losses over a race distance. Small gains in efficiency translate directly into more usable energy in the final laps, or the ability to push harder when it matters.

The second part is test benches. Valeo will provide high precision benches to fine-tune and stress-test the powertrain's core electronics. A test bench lets engineers run the motor and inverter through repeatable load cycles, measure efficiency maps, check thermal behaviour and find weaknesses before they appear on track.

Mahindra describes this as a race to road approach. The same disciplines, precise control, minimal losses and rigorous testing, apply directly to production electric cars, where efficiency means more range from the same battery.

For students, this story is a good reminder that an E V powertrain is as much about software and power electronics as it is about the motor itself. If you want to go deeper, study field-oriented control, space vector modulation, and how inverter losses are split between conduction and switching.

The full press release from Mahindra is linked on this page.

items.title: Toyota Develops New Hybrid for Future Multi-Pathway Vehicle Platforms
items.summary: Toyota's next hybrid system is designed for platforms that keep several powertrain options open at once.
items.script:
Toyota has described a new hybrid system for its future multi-pathway vehicle platforms. It is built around a new family of one point five litre, four-cylinder engines, in naturally aspirated and turbocharged versions. The engine, electric motors, power control units and inverters are developed together as a single compact package, designed to reduce both electrical and mechanical losses. Toyota is targeting more than fifteen percent better fuel economy, through lower friction, better thermal management, lower electrical losses and less aerodynamic drag.

The phrase multi-pathway is central to Toyota's strategy. Instead of betting only on battery electric vehicles, Toyota is designing a common architecture that can carry battery electric, plug-in hybrid and conventional hybrid powertrains. Because the new engine and hybrid unit are compact, they allow lower bonnet lines, so the same body can accept different powertrains. That lets factories change the production mix as demand shifts and spreads development costs across larger volumes.

Why does integrating the motor, inverter and engine matter? In a hybrid, energy is constantly converted: chemical energy in fuel becomes mechanical work, which can become electrical energy in the generator, which is stored in the battery and then converted back to motion by the motor. Every conversion loses a little energy, in the inverter's switching transistors, in the motor windings and in the wiring between components. Placing them close together shortens cables, reduces losses and saves weight. Shared cooling circuits also help with thermal management, which is critical for both power electronics and the engine.

Toyota's hybrids typically use a power split device, a planetary gearset that blends engine and motor power without a conventional gearbox. The power control unit, with its inverter and boost converter, decides moment by moment how power flows. Much of the efficiency gain in a new generation comes from improving these electronics and the control strategy, not just the engine.

Toyota also says the system is being developed to run on renewable and carbon-neutral fuels, and that it plans to sell the new engine and hybrid technology to other companies. It reports more than thirty five million electrified vehicles sold to date.

For students, this is a good case study in system-level optimisation, where the biggest gains come from how components work together.

The full article from Electronic Design is linked on this page.

trends.title: ECUs, cameras and the electronics supply chain
trends.summary: Camera modules, engine control modules and cockpit electronics are changing hands, and new electronics manufacturing ventures are forming, from Sahasra's Asetronics deal in India to a Hongfa and VinFast components plant in Vietnam. AI servers now compete with cars for circuit-board capacity, capital needs are pushing smaller players out, and CT scanning and self-calibrating sensors aim to cut defects and end-of-line work.

items.title: Hongfa and VinFast joint venture opens automotive electronics plant in northern Vietnam
items.summary: HFVF, a joint venture between China's Hongfa Group and Vietnamese carmaker VinFast, has opened a factory for automotive electronic components in northern Vietnam. The move puts part of the electronics supply chain next to VinFast's own vehicle production.
items.script:
A new automotive electronics factory has opened in northern Vietnam. According to The Investor, the plant belongs to H F V F, a joint venture between China's Hongfa Group and the Vietnamese carmaker VinFast. The factory makes automotive electronic components. The story is a small but clear sign of how carmakers are building local electronics supply chains around their vehicle plants. VinFast builds electric cars in Vietnam, and this partnership gives it a component source close to home, run with an experienced Chinese supplier.

Hongfa is best known worldwide as a maker of relays, so it is worth asking why relays still matter in a modern car. A relay is an electrically controlled switch. A small current through a coil moves a contact that switches a much larger current. Cars use dozens of them for loads such as cooling fans, fuel pumps, seat heaters, horns and lamps, usually grouped in a fuse and relay box under the bonnet. Many of these jobs are moving to semiconductor switches, but relays remain cheap, robust and give true galvanic isolation.

In an electric vehicle, the most important relatives of the relay are high voltage contactors. These connect and disconnect the traction battery from the rest of the car. A typical battery pack has a main positive contactor, a main negative contactor and a pre charge circuit. The pre charge path closes first through a resistor, so the large capacitors in the inverter charge slowly. Only then do the main contactors close. Without this step, the inrush current could weld the contacts together. Contactors must also break high direct current safely during a crash or fault, which is harder than switching alternating current, because there is no natural zero crossing to quench the arc.

Any factory supplying parts like these must meet strict quality rules. The I A T F sixteen nine four nine standard covers the quality system of automotive suppliers. Passive and electromechanical parts are usually qualified to A E C Q two hundred, which defines stress tests such as temperature cycling, humidity and vibration.

Local production also cuts logistics risk and shipping time, and helps carmakers meet local content targets, which many countries now link to tax breaks and other incentives. For a young carmaker, a nearby partner can also speed up design changes.

For students, battery disconnect units, pre charge design and contactor diagnostics are excellent topics to explore next. The full report from The Investor is linked on this page.

items.title: Infineon introduces digital angle sensors with automatic calibration
items.summary: Infineon has released a family of digital angle sensors that calibrate themselves, with automotive-qualified versions sold as the TLE49012. The aim is to cut the end-of-line calibration work that position sensors normally need in motors and actuators.
items.script:
Infineon has introduced a new family of digital angle sensors that can calibrate themselves automatically. The automotive qualified versions carry the part number T L E four nine zero one two, and according to the report they are designed to comply with I S O requirements for automotive use. The news was carried by Military and Aerospace Electronics. The source page could not be opened for this overview, so the details here are limited to the published summary, and the rest of this overview explains the technology behind it.

An angle sensor tells a controller exactly where a rotating shaft is pointing. In a car, that information is needed everywhere. The electric power steering system needs the angle of the steering column and of its motor. A brushless motor in a pump, fan or electric drive needs the rotor position so the inverter can switch the phases at the right moment. Throttle bodies, pedal modules and gear selectors also use angle sensing.

Most of these sensors are magnetic. A small magnet is fixed to the end of the shaft, and a sensor chip sits just beneath it. As the shaft turns, the direction of the magnetic field turns with it. The chip measures two field components at right angles, roughly a sine and a cosine, and computes the angle from them using an arctangent calculation, often done with the CORDIC algorithm. The sensing element can be a Hall plate, or a magnetoresistive element such as anisotropic, giant or tunnel magnetoresistance, each with its own trade offs in sensitivity, noise and temperature drift.

The weak spot is calibration. In a real assembly the magnet is never perfectly centred, the two channels have slightly different gains and offsets, and the signals are not exactly ninety degrees apart. Traditionally each unit is calibrated at the end of the production line, which costs time and test equipment. Automatic calibration moves that job into the chip, which learns and corrects these errors while it runs.

Digital output matters too. Interfaces such as S E N T or S P C send the angle as a robust digital message instead of an analog voltage, which reduces noise problems on long wires. For safety related uses such as steering, the sensor must also support I S O twenty six two six two, usually with diagnostics and sometimes with two independent sensing dies in one package.

If you study motor control, angle sensing is worth learning in depth. The full report from Military and Aerospace Electronics is linked on this page.

items.title: Industrial CT and AI expose hidden defects in automotive electrical connectors
items.summary: A report on how industrial X-ray computed tomography, paired with AI analysis, can find faults inside automotive connectors that visual and electrical checks miss.
items.script:
Electronics For You Business has reported on the use of industrial computed tomography, combined with artificial intelligence, to find hidden defects inside automotive electrical connectors. The story came through as a short alert, so the companies involved and the specific findings are described in the linked article. Here we focus on why connectors matter and how this inspection method works.

A modern car contains hundreds of connectors and several thousand contact points. Every sensor, actuator and control unit depends on them. Field studies have long shown that a large share of electrical faults in vehicles come not from the chips, but from wiring and connections. The trouble is that many connector faults cannot be seen from outside. A terminal may look fully seated while it is slightly crooked inside its housing. A crimp may pass a pull test but contain voids. A locking latch may be cracked under the plastic.

Computed tomography, or C T, is the same principle used in hospital scanners. The part is placed on a rotating stage between an X ray source and a detector. Hundreds or thousands of images are taken from different angles. Software then reconstructs a full three dimensional model, showing the inside of the part, slice by slice, without cutting it open.

The challenge is the amount of data. One scan can produce gigabytes of volume information. That is where A I comes in. Machine learning models can segment the image, separating metal terminals from plastic housing, and then flag anomalies such as gaps, misalignments, porosity or foreign particles. This makes the analysis faster and more consistent than a human inspector scrolling through slices.

Connector quality is tightly specified. Standards such as U S C A R two in North America and L V two one four in Germany define tests for vibration, temperature cycling, humidity and mating forces. In electric vehicles, high voltage connectors add more risk, because a poor contact can overheat at hundreds of amps. They also include interlock pins that tell the battery system when a plug is opened.

Small faults lead to intermittent problems, such as fretting corrosion that comes and goes with vibration. These are the hardest faults to diagnose in a workshop, because the car often behaves perfectly by the time a technician connects a tester.

For students, connectors are a reminder that reliability depends on mechanics as much as electronics. The full report from Electronics For You Business is linked on this page.

items.title: Sahasra promoters form 55:45 Asetronics manufacturing venture
items.summary: The promoters of Sahasra are setting up a 55:45 joint venture with Asetronics to manufacture electronics for automotive, medical, industrial and railway customers in Europe and India.
items.script:
The promoters of Sahasra, an Indian semiconductor company, have formed a manufacturing joint venture with Asetronics. The split is fifty-five to forty-five. The new company, Sahasra Asetronics, will target electronics manufacturing for automotive, medical, industrial and railway customers, in both Europe and India. Our information comes from a brief market alert, and the source page could not be retrieved, so details such as investment, location and timing are not confirmed here. The story still says a lot about how vehicle electronics actually get built.

Most car electronics are not assembled by the carmaker, or even by the brand on the E C U label. They are often built by electronics manufacturing services companies, known as E M S providers. An E M S plant takes a bare printed circuit board and turns it into a working module.

The heart of that process is surface mount technology. A stencil prints solder paste onto the pads. High-speed pick-and-place machines set thousands of components per hour. The board then passes through a reflow oven, where a carefully controlled temperature profile melts the solder. After that come inspections: automated optical inspection to check placement, X-ray for hidden joints under ball grid array packages, and in-circuit or functional testing to prove the module works. Many automotive boards also receive a conformal coating to protect against moisture and contamination.

Automotive work adds strict rules. Plants are certified to I A T F sixteen nine four nine, and workmanship is judged against I P C A six ten, usually at the highest reliability class. Every board must be traceable, so a failure in the field can be linked back to the component lot, the machine and even the oven profile used on that day. Medical work follows I S O thirteen four eight five, and railway electronics have their own standard, E N fifty one fifty five, for vibration, temperature and supply variation.

Serving these four sectors together makes sense, because they share the same need for high reliability and long product lifetimes.

There is a strategic angle too. Governments in Europe and India both want more electronics production closer to home after the supply shocks of recent years. A venture that links an Indian semiconductor business with an electronics manufacturer could shorten the path from packaged chip to finished, tested module.

For students, this is a good prompt to learn design for manufacturing and test. The full report from Multibagg AI is linked on this page.

items.title: Global Electronics Association warns AI server boards are crowding out auto, medical and other sectors
items.summary: The industry body has issued an alert that demand for AI server boards is squeezing printed circuit board supply for cars and medical devices. It warns the crunch could rival the 2021 chip shortage.
items.script:
The Global Electronics Association has issued an industry alert about printed circuit boards. Its warning is that boards for artificial intelligence servers are taking up so much manufacturing capacity that other sectors, including automotive and medical, are being crowded out. The association says this supply crunch could rival the chip shortage of twenty twenty-one. The report came to us through a short news alert, and the original article could not be retrieved, so we do not have lead times or price figures. Let's focus on why boards matter and why cars are exposed.

A printed circuit board, or P C B, is the layered structure that carries and connects every chip in an E C U. It is built from copper foil laminated onto glass-fibre fabric impregnated with resin. Simple boards have two or four layers. A modern A D A S domain controller or central computer may use many more, with very fine lines and microvias, a style called high density interconnect.

A I server boards are at the extreme end. They are large, have very high layer counts, and need premium low-loss laminates to carry high-speed signals. Each one consumes a lot of press time, drilling capacity and specialised material. When fabricators can sell that capacity at a high margin, lower-margin work waits in the queue.

Automotive buyers cannot simply switch to another board shop. Every automotive P C B is qualified for a specific design. The supplier must work under I A T F sixteen nine four nine quality management, and changes go through a production part approval process, or P P A P. Boards must survive thermal cycling, vibration and humidity for fifteen years or more, so materials and processes are locked once approved. Requalifying a new source can take months.

That is exactly what made twenty twenty-one so painful. A missing part worth a few cents stopped entire vehicle lines, because nothing else was approved to replace it.

There is also a design angle. As cars move towards zonal architectures and central computers, automotive boards start to look more like server boards. Higher layer counts, fast serial links for cameras and multi-gigabit Ethernet all call for the same premium laminates. So the competition for capacity is likely to grow, not shrink.

For engineers, the lesson is design for resilience: second-source qualification, standard stack-ups, and close monitoring of materials such as laminate and glass fabric. The full report from AI News is linked on this page.

items.title: BorgWarner Secures Engine Control Module Business With Major Global OEM
items.summary: BorgWarner PowerDrive Systems has won an engine control module programme with a large global OEM. Combustion and hybrid ECUs are still a live business.
items.script:
BorgWarner has won a high-volume contract to supply engine control modules for an internal combustion pick-up truck platform from a long-standing global carmaker. BorgWarner has supplied engine control modules to this customer since 2020, and the new deal extends the relationship to 2034, with production expected to start in 2029.

The engine control module, often called the E C M or engine E C U, is the brain of a combustion engine. It reads sensors such as crankshaft and camshaft position, manifold pressure, air mass flow, coolant temperature and the oxygen sensors in the exhaust. From these, it calculates exactly how much fuel to inject, when to inject it, when to fire the spark plugs and how to control the throttle, turbocharger and exhaust gas recirculation. It does this for every cylinder, every cycle, while keeping emissions within legal limits.

According to the report, this E C M was designed specifically for the platform, with more functions, more flexible control, and a compact layout. It can control diesel, gasoline direct injection and port fuel injection engines, and works with all injectors currently on the market. It uses BorgWarner's own application-specific integrated circuits, an advanced microprocessor, and integrated control of exhaust aftertreatment. Its direct injection control supports fuel pressures of five hundred bar.

Why does five hundred bar matter? In gasoline direct injection, fuel is sprayed straight into the cylinder. Higher pressure produces finer droplets, which mix better with air and burn more completely, reducing particulate emissions. But driving injectors at those pressures needs high-voltage, precisely timed current pulses. That is why custom chips are used: they handle the injector drive stages that a general-purpose microcontroller cannot.

Aftertreatment control is the other big task. Catalytic converters, particulate filters and, on diesels, selective catalytic reduction systems all need precise management, and emissions rules keep tightening.

There is a wider lesson here. While electric vehicles get the headlines, combustion and hybrid powertrains will remain in production for many years, especially in pick-up trucks and commercial vehicles. Engine management remains a busy field for embedded engineers.

BorgWarner's portfolio also includes battery management, motor, transmission and commercial vehicle engine controllers, showing how suppliers are spreading across both combustion and electric technologies.

The full report from Motor India is linked on this page.

items.title: Foxconn acquires automotive camera module business from Sony Semiconductor Solutions
items.summary: Foxconn (Hon Hai) is buying Sony's automotive camera module business to grow in ADAS sensing. The initial deal is valued at about ¥7.2 billion (~$45 million).
items.script:
Foxconn, the Taiwanese electronics manufacturer also known as Hon Hai, has agreed to acquire the automotive camera module business of Sony Semiconductor Solutions. The deal includes the business's technology, its customer base, and its experience of supplying carmakers directly. Closing is expected by the end of April 2027, subject to regulatory approval. Reports put the initial transaction at about seven point two billion yen, roughly forty five million U S dollars. Sony's relevant overseas entities will provide transitional support after closing, with the focus on keeping customer service and operations stable.

Why would Foxconn want this? Foxconn already builds huge numbers of camera modules for smartphones and other consumer electronics. Cars are a growing market for cameras.
