A modern vehicle may carry several of them: a forward camera behind the windscreen for lane keeping and automatic emergency braking, surround-view cameras for parking, rear cameras, and increasingly an interior camera that monitors whether the driver is paying attention. Advanced driver assistance systems depend on these sensors, and demand grows with every new safety regulation.

An automotive camera module is more than a lens and an image sensor. It includes the sensor chip, optics, a circuit board with a serialiser that sends high-speed video over a coaxial cable, and a sealed housing that must survive heat, cold, vibration and water for many years. Automotive image sensors also need high dynamic range, so they can see clearly when driving out of a dark tunnel into bright sunlight, and they must handle flickering L E D traffic lights. Quality requirements are strict, with automotive qualification standards and functional safety considerations.

It is worth noting what Sony is not selling. Sony remains a leading maker of automotive image sensors, the chips inside the camera. This deal concerns the module business, which assembles those sensors into complete camera units. Foxconn's strength in high-volume precision assembly fits that layer of the supply chain.

The deal also fits Foxconn's broader push into vehicles, including its electric vehicle platform efforts. Owning more of the electronics supply chain lets it offer carmakers more complete systems.

For engineers, this is a reminder that sensing hardware is a strategic part of the vehicle, and that consolidation among suppliers is changing who builds what.

The full report is linked on this page.

items.title: Large capital needs, technology shift behind Pricol Autotech exit, says Vikram Mohan
items.summary: Pricol's promoter family is selling its entire stake, saying the automotive electronics business now needs more capital to stay competitive.
items.script:
The promoter family of Pricol, an Indian automotive component maker, is selling its entire holding in Pricol Autotech, the company's automotive electronics business, which is being demerged into a separate listed company. The buyer is the private equity firm Warburg Pincus. According to the report, Warburg would acquire about thirty eight and a half percent of the demerged company's equity, in a deal worth up to one thousand six hundred and sixty three crore rupees. Chairman Vikram Mohan said the family could not fund the heavy, continuing investment the business needs in technology, manufacturing and talent while keeping majority ownership. He will step down as chairman and managing director of Autotech once the transfer completes, and the current senior team will stay.

This is a useful lens on the economics of automotive electronics. Pricol is known for instrument clusters and other electronic products. Twenty years ago, an instrument cluster was a set of analogue gauges with a few warning lamps. Today it is often a high-resolution digital display, driven by a graphics processor, running a real-time operating system, connected to the vehicle network, and sometimes merged with the infotainment screen into a single cockpit domain controller.

Each step of that evolution raises the cost of staying competitive. You need software teams, displays and graphics expertise, cybersecurity processes, functional safety certification, and the ability to deliver over-the-air updates. Product cycles are shorter, and customers expect suppliers to co-develop features. All of that requires sustained investment, often ahead of revenue.

Mohan said a buyer with deeper finances, stronger management expertise and global reach was better placed to take the business forward. That pattern is visible across the industry. Electronics businesses tend to consolidate, because scale spreads the large fixed costs of software and validation.

Meanwhile, Pricol's remaining businesses are expanding with internal funds and borrowing. These include new plants in Sanand and Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, recently commissioned plants in Mysuru and Narsapura, a large plant in Hosur, and a polymer engineering centre in Coimbatore.

For students and engineers, the takeaway is that automotive electronics is a capital-intensive, fast-moving field. The value increasingly lies in software and system integration, and that is where investment, and hiring, are concentrating.

The full report is linked on this page.

trends.title: Shared platforms and standardisation
trends.summary: To cut cost and development time, carmakers are sharing platforms and agreeing on common parts. In China, a shared standard is being written for drive-by-wire chassis, and suppliers such as FORVIA HELLA are shipping second-generation brake-by-wire pedals to Chinese customers.

items.title: FORVIA HELLA introduces second-generation brake-by-wire pedal
items.summary: FORVIA HELLA has shown a second-generation pedal for brake-by-wire systems, developed by its engineering team in Germany. It is aimed at several Chinese automotive technology companies.
items.script:
The German supplier FORVIA HELLA has introduced the second generation of its brake by wire pedal. According to The Brake Report, the pedal was developed by the supplier's headquarters team in Germany. It will serve several Chinese automotive technology companies and other customers in China. This story came through as a short alert, so the detailed specifications are in the linked article.

In a conventional car, the brake pedal pushes a rod into a vacuum booster and a master cylinder. Hydraulic pressure then flows through pipes to the brake callipers. The driver's foot is physically connected to the brakes.

Brake by wire breaks that link. The pedal becomes an electronic sensor. It measures how far and how hard the driver presses and sends that request as a signal to a brake controller. The controller then builds braking force using an electric pump, an electro hydraulic unit, or in future, fully electro mechanical callipers at each wheel.

Taking away the physical link creates two engineering challenges. The first is feel. Drivers expect the pedal to push back in a familiar way. So a by wire pedal includes a pedal feel simulator, usually a set of springs and dampers, sometimes with active elements, that recreates the progressive resistance of a hydraulic system.

The second challenge is safety. If the signal is lost, the car must still stop. So the pedal uses redundant sensors, often two independent position sensors based on different principles, such as inductive and Hall effect sensing. Their signals travel over separate channels with separate power supplies. The design is developed under I S O twenty six two six two, typically to the highest level, A S I L D, and braking systems must also meet the U N regulations for brakes.

Why go to this trouble? By wire braking makes regenerative braking much smoother in electric cars, because software can blend motor braking and friction braking without the driver feeling the switch. It also frees up space in the front bulkhead, simplifies assembly across left and right hand drive, and lets automated driving functions command the brakes directly. Without hydraulic lines running to the pedal, carmakers can also reuse the same braking module across many vehicle models.

That explains the interest from Chinese companies, who are pushing hard on drive by wire chassis platforms. For students, study redundancy concepts and fault tolerant sensor design next. The full report from The Brake Report is linked on this page.

items.title: From Flagship to Standard: Drive-by-Wire Chassis on a "Long Run"
items.summary: China is writing a standard for drive-by-wire chassis, led by SAIC Motor with NIO, CATARC, Li Auto and XPENG among the co-drafters. By-wire steering and braking are moving from flagship models towards wider use.
items.script:
Gasgoo, the Chinese automotive news service, reports that drive-by-wire chassis technology is moving from flagship cars towards becoming standard equipment, and that a standard for it is being written. SAIC Motor led the drafting. The joint drafters include NIO, Li Auto, XPENG and the China Automotive Technology and Research Center, known as C A T A R C. The alert we received did not give the standard's number or its dates, so we will stick to what is confirmed. What we can do is explain what drive-by-wire means and why it needs a common rulebook.

In a conventional car, your hands and feet are mechanically or hydraulically connected to the wheels. The steering column turns a rack. The brake pedal pushes fluid through a master cylinder. Electronics only assist. In a by-wire chassis, that physical link is replaced by sensors, wires and actuators. Turning the wheel produces an electrical signal. A control unit reads it and commands an electric motor at the steering rack. Pressing the pedal sends a signal that tells an electro-hydraulic or fully electro-mechanical brake how hard to clamp.

The benefits are real. Software can change the steering ratio with speed. Brakes can blend smoothly with regenerative braking in an electric car. Automated driving functions can steer and stop the car directly. Packaging becomes easier because there is no column or vacuum booster in the way.

The challenge is safety. If the mechanical backup is gone, the electronics must keep working even after a fault. Engineers call this fail-operational design. It usually means redundant sensors, two independent power supplies, two communication paths, and actuators with duplicated windings or a second channel. The development process follows I S O twenty six two six two, and steering and braking functions are typically rated at the highest integrity level, A S I L D. Timing on the in-vehicle network matters too, because a delayed message is as dangerous as a lost one. Fault detection has to happen within milliseconds, so the backup channel can take over before the driver notices anything. That is why these systems favour deterministic communication with tightly scheduled messages.

A shared national standard helps carmakers and suppliers agree on test methods, redundancy requirements and performance limits. It also gives regulators a basis for type approval, which is the gate any by-wire system must pass before it reaches mass production.

If this interests you, study redundancy architectures and fault-tolerant control. The full report from Gasgoo is linked on this page.

items.title: Toyota, Nissan, Honda back Japan plan to standardize parts, lower costs
items.summary: Japan's carmakers association (JAMA) proposes industry-wide parts standards. No timeline has been given yet.
items.script:
Japan's carmakers, including Toyota, Nissan and Honda, are backing an industry plan to standardise vehicle parts in order to lower costs. The plan comes from the Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association, known as JAMA. According to the report, no concrete timeline has been set yet for implementing the standardisation goals.

Why would fierce competitors agree to share parts? The answer lies in rising costs. Each new generation of vehicles adds more electronics, more software, and more development work for safety, emissions and cybersecurity regulations. At the same time, Japanese carmakers face strong price competition, especially from Chinese manufacturers who have moved quickly in electric vehicles and in-car software. When every company designs its own version of a part that customers never see, the industry pays for the same engineering many times over.

Standardisation is not new in the automotive world. Connectors, fasteners, diagnostic interfaces such as the O B D port, and communication protocols such as C A N are all standardised, which is why tools and components work across brands. AUTOSAR is another example: carmakers and suppliers agreed on a common software architecture for control units, so that suppliers can reuse software and carmakers can integrate it more easily. Competition then shifts to the features that customers actually notice.

For electronics, standard parts could mean common semiconductors, shared control unit hardware, or common interfaces between components. That would help suppliers achieve larger production volumes, which lowers unit costs and can make supply chains more resilient. The semiconductor shortage of recent years showed how vulnerable the industry is when many slightly different chips are each made in small quantities.

There are trade-offs. Standards take time to agree, and companies worry about losing differentiation. Deciding which parts are truly non-differentiating is often the hardest part of such efforts, which may explain the lack of a timeline.

For engineers, standardisation is a reminder that good interfaces are as important as good components. If you are designing a module, thinking about how it fits into a standard architecture makes it far more valuable.

The full report from Automotive News is linked on this page.

items.title: Tata Group draws Honda and Hyundai interest in vehicle and tech sharing
items.summary: Honda and Hyundai are reported to be exploring platform and technology sharing with Tata.
items.script:
Reports say Honda and Hyundai are exploring opportunities to share vehicles, platforms and technology with the Tata Group. The report describes global manufacturers looking at cooperation with the Indian automotive major, rather than any agreement that has been signed.

Platform and technology sharing has become common across the global industry, and it is worth understanding why. A vehicle platform is the shared engineering foundation underneath a car: the floor structure, suspension layout, powertrain mounting, and increasingly the electrical and electronic architecture. Developing a new platform costs a great deal of money and takes several years. Sharing it across more models and more brands spreads that cost over more vehicles.

Electrification makes sharing even more attractive. Battery electric platforms, battery packs, motors and power electronics require heavy investment, and suppliers offer better prices for larger volumes. Tata Motors has invested significantly in electric vehicles for the Indian market, and Tata Group companies also have strengths in software and engineering services. For a global carmaker, partnering in India can provide access to cost-competitive engineering, local manufacturing and an understanding of the Indian market, which is one of the largest in the world.

Software is a growing part of these discussions. In a software-defined vehicle, the electronic architecture, the operating system and the cloud services are expensive to build and maintain. Several carmakers around the world now share software stacks or collaborate on them, rather than each building everything alone.

There are challenges, of course. Partners must agree on which parts are shared and which remain unique to each brand, protect their intellectual property, and align development schedules. Sharing electronics also means aligning cybersecurity and functional safety processes, so that each partner can certify the vehicle under its own responsibility.

For engineers and students in India, partnerships like these could mean more global programmes developed locally, with Indian teams working on platforms used around the world.

As always with reports of early-stage talks, it is best to treat this as a direction of travel rather than a done deal.

The full report from Team-B H P is linked on this page.

items.title: 2027 Hyundai ELANTRA and 2028 ELANTRA Hybrid Revealed at Los Angeles Auto Show
items.summary: The eighth-generation Elantra adds more connectivity and driver-assistance features.
items.script:
Hyundai has revealed the eighth-generation 2027 Elantra and the 2028 Elantra Hybrid at the Los Angeles Auto Show. Beyond the new design, the electronics upgrades are significant.

Start with the cockpit. Every trim gets a twelve point nine inch full H D touchscreen running Hyundai's Pleos Connect infotainment platform, which is built on Android Automotive. Wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto are supported. Connectivity includes cloud services, a Wi-Fi hotspot and Hyundai's app ecosystem. There is a new voice assistant called Gleo A I, built on a large language model, which can handle several commands at once and recognise whether the driver or a passenger is speaking. Software and feature updates can be delivered over the air, without a visit to the dealer. Hyundai has kept physical buttons and knobs for audio and climate, a choice many drivers appreciate.

Android Automotive is worth explaining. Unlike Android Auto, which projects your phone onto the car's screen, Android Automotive is an operating system that runs directly on the car's own computer. The carmaker customises it and connects it to vehicle functions. It is one of the clearest signs of how consumer software platforms are moving into vehicles.

On safety, the SmartSense suite includes forward collision avoidance that can detect pedestrians, cyclists, and vehicles when turning at junctions or coming the other way. It also has blind-spot and rear cross-traffic warnings, lane keeping with haptic feedback, adaptive cruise control with stop and go, and on top trims, a driver monitoring system that checks whether the driver is paying attention. These features rely on fusing data from cameras and radar sensors.

The hybrid gets a meaningful upgrade. The 2028 Elantra Hybrid combines a one point six litre engine with a six-speed dual clutch transmission, for one hundred and fifty five horsepower combined, up from one hundred and thirty nine. The electric motor grows from thirty two to forty five kilowatts, and the battery from one point three two to one point four nine kilowatt hours. Hyundai targets up to fifty three miles per gallon combined, though that is not yet an official rating. A stay mode can run the climate, audio and lights from the hybrid battery for around twenty to thirty minutes while parked.

For students, this mainstream sedan shows how quickly over-the-air updates, A I assistants and sensor fusion have become standard features.

The full press release is linked on this page.
